name: Brick
subcategory: app blocking with a physical unlock
tagline: An iOS app blocker that only unlocks when you physically tap a magnet-mounted NFC tag you left at home.

pricing.plan: Brick device, one-time purchase, app is free
pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The software here is thin: Apple's own Screen Time frameworks do the blocking, and CoreNFC does the tap. An agent can write you a SwiftUI app that shields a chosen set of apps and only lifts the shield when a specific NFC tag UID is scanned, and that is genuinely most of the product. The friction is all Apple's: you need a Mac, Xcode, a paid developer account to keep the build on your phone, and the Family Controls entitlement, which is a request to Apple rather than a checkbox. You also need to buy an NFC tag and stick it somewhere inconvenient, which is the part Brick actually sells. So the answer is yes in code and kinda in practice.
coreLoopDIY: A local iOS app that shields a user-picked set of apps and websites indefinitely, and only unshields when you scan one specific NFC tag.
requirements: An Apple Developer account so the build does not expire every seven days
Family Controls entitlement request approved by Apple
Any cheap NTAG213 sticker or an adhesive NFC tag
An iPhone running a recent iOS
whatYouLose: The physical object: a weighted, magnetic, deliberately annoying thing that is the entire behavioral trick
Polish around the edge cases: emergency unlocks, timed sessions, streaks, and the nag screens that make the shield feel final
Cross-device and cross-OS parity if you ever leave iPhone
Updates when Apple changes the Screen Time frameworks, which it does
App Store review as a sanity check that the thing will not brick your phone in a way you did not intend
moatNotes: The code is commodity Apple API glue. The product is a tangible object you can walk away from, plus the confidence that an app with deep device-restriction power is not going to misbehave.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the hard part of a focus tool is not blocking apps, it is making the unblock expensive enough to matter. Brick sells a physical commitment device, and a self-signed build you can delete in twelve seconds with no adhesive tag on the fridge is a much weaker promise. Add the developer account cost, the entitlement paperwork, and the fact that you will maintain it yourself every time iOS shifts, and the one-time device price stops looking like a rip-off.
notes: The honest low-effort version is an iOS Shortcuts NFC automation plus a Focus mode, no code at all, and it works well enough that you should try it before opening Xcode.
prompt:
Build a single-target iOS app called TapToUnblock using SwiftUI and Swift 5.9, minimum iOS 17, no backend, no accounts, no analytics.
Purpose: block a chosen set of apps and website categories indefinitely, and only lift the block when a specific physical NFC tag is scanned.
Use Apple's Screen Time frameworks: FamilyControls for the app picker, ManagedSettings for applying the shield, and DeviceActivity only if needed for reporting.
On first launch, request Family Controls authorization for the individual (not child) case and show a clear error state if it is denied.
Provide a FamilyActivityPicker screen so the user selects apps, categories, and web domains to block. Persist the selection to disk with Codable plus FileManager in the app group container.
Apply the selection via ManagedSettingsStore shieldSettings when the user taps "Start blocking".
Use CoreNFC to read NDEF or tag UID. Add a "Pair tag" flow that stores one tag identifier in the Keychain as the only valid unlock key.
When blocking is active, the only way to clear the ManagedSettingsStore is a successful scan of the paired tag. No password fallback, no timer fallback, no "are you sure" escape hatch.
Add one deliberate exception: a hard-coded 10 minute grace unlock that can only be used once per 24 hours, tracked locally, so a lost tag does not trap the user forever.
UI: three screens only. Home showing blocked/unblocked state and a big Scan button, Picker, and Settings for tag pairing. Plain SF Symbols, no custom design system.
Entitlements: add com.apple.developer.family-controls and Near Field Communication Tag Reading to the target. Add NFCReaderUsageDescription to Info.plist. Note in the README that the Family Controls entitlement must be requested from Apple and that a paid developer account is needed to avoid 7 day build expiry.
No secrets are needed, but create .env.example and a README anyway documenting the Apple account, bundle ID, and app group ID the developer must substitute.
Out of scope: App Store packaging, iCloud sync, widgets, streaks, social features, Android, macOS.
Deliver the Xcode project, all Swift sources, and a README with exact build steps and the known failure modes: denied authorization, missing entitlement, and NFC unavailable on simulator.
Add a short section to the README explaining how to test without a real tag by stubbing the scan result behind a DEBUG flag.
